text:
Dear @HDFC_Bank @HDFCBank_Cares,

Recently, I applied for a Home Loan of ₹50 Lakhs (File No: 705118170) for a flat valued at ₹75 Lakhs near Ganapathi Complex, Srinagar Colony, Hyderabad. It is a 30-year-old apartment. Despite my clean financial profile—a 770 CIBIL score, zero active liabilities, a regular monthly salary of ₹1 Lakh credited to my bank account, and a flawless track record as a law-abiding taxpayer—HDFC quoted me an exorbitant interest rate of 10.25%. After making me run around for numerous documents and conducting multiple verifications, your team casually tagged my profile under a "Risk Zone."

In stark contrast, the Bank of Maharashtra issued an in-principle sanction letter at a highly competitive interest rate of 7.25% for the exact same property and profile, that too with zero processing fees.

This raises serious questions about your lending ecosystem:

Why is there a massive 3% interest rate discrepancy between HDFC (10.25%) and Bank of Maharashtra (7.25%)? If my profile poses a risk to HDFC, why did a nationalized bank find it perfectly safe?

HDFC collected ₹2,400 as processing fees, and I ended up spending nearly ₹4,000 in total overhead expenses. Yet, I have not even received an in-principle sanction letter. Is it fair to pocket non-refundable processing fees from customers before providing any formal loan approval?

To add to the ordeal, your ground verification representatives openly demanded bribes. Is this the standard operating procedure and corporate governance HDFC takes pride in?

Every single day, thousands of middle-class citizens apply for home loans across the country. Many cancel their applications due to such arbitrary pricing and high-handedness. What happens to the crores of rupees collected daily under the tag of 'non-refundable' processing fees? When a bank fails to offer a fair deal or when a customer withdraws due to exploitation, shouldn't that money be legally refunded? Or has this become a lucrative parallel business model for private banks?

It is disheartening to see how major banking institutions turn a blind eye when multi-crore corporate defaulters fleece the system and flee the country, yet subject an honest, salaried middle-class individual to endless scrutiny and harassment. A home loan is not charity; it is a commercial transaction where the customer repays every rupee with interest, and the property documents remain mortgaged as collateral with the bank until the final tenure.

Prominent institutions like HDFC must realize that winning the trust of a middle-class consumer is a much bigger asset than squeezing them with unfair interest rates. It is high time that banking regulatory authorities step in to monitor and curtail this interest rate blackmail by private banks.

I demand a transparent explanation and accountability regarding my application.

Ashok Vemulapalli

There are many outstanding bankers fully capable of professionally managing and cleaning up rut in the @HDFC_Bank. Instead, the bank has appointed a former civil servant with no banking background — retired IAS officer and former Chief Election Commissioner Rajiv Kumar — as its Chairman.

This appointment appears to have been nudged by the political government for two clear reasons. 

First, it rewards Rajiv Kumar for his role in allegedly converting the Election Commission into a front organisation for the BJP. As a former CEC, he could not have been given another government position without inviting severe criticism.

Second, it gives the political government greater influence over one of India’s largest private-sector banks, allowing it to advance their own private financial interests.

Therefore, placing him in a high-profile non-government role to head HDFC Bank is a #Masterstroke by the political government to achieve both objectives simultaneously.

Lastly, at least since 2014, high-profile appointments in major corporates, including private banks and financial institutions, are rarely made without the political government being taken into confidence.

Rumours travel fast. Facts, unfortunately, take their time.

Until then, I remain curious.

I am writing to express my strong dissatisfaction regarding the rejection of my credit card application (Reference No. D26F27027441S0P0).

The representative only asked for my office address and whether I was present at the office before abruptly disconnecting the call. I have now received a notification stating that my application was declined due to "Business Address Verification norms not met."

It is unacceptable that an application is rejected without any actual physical verification being conducted. Calling to solicit applications and then providing arbitrary reasons for rejection after a long processing period is highly unprofessional.

I request a thorough review of this decision and a proper verification process.

Regards,

Rajan Chaudhary

text:

text:
Dear @HDFCBank_Cares,

Please train your branch managers and staff... especially in rural and suburban branches on how to handle inward remittances and forex transactions.

Instead of verifying the facts, I was met with assumptions and treated like I was involved in fraud, without any evidence or explanation. They kept telling me how scammers operate and why my transaction could be fraudulent, rather than investigating my case or listening to my explanation.

Being a student doesn't mean I can't legitimately earn money through software engineering, freelancing, hackathons, or international projects. Customers deserve to be treated with respect, not judged based on their age or profession.

Also, I don't believe this is a Forex Department issue. I know several people with HDFC Bank accounts at different branches who received inward remittances from the same remitter, and their transactions were processed and credited within two hours.

This appears to be a branch-level issue caused by a lack of awareness and training, not a problem with the remittance itself. I hope HDFC ensures that branch staff are properly trained to handle legitimate international remittances professionally, without making baseless assumptions or inconveniencing customers.

text:
Something’s really rotten at @HDFC_Bank. Their tech systems are just broken. 

I had made an Airbnb booking in April using an HDFC credit card. The booking was cancelled in June, and my credit card statement for June also showed the transaction reversal. I had called HDFC’s customer care, and they also confirmed that the booking cancellation amount was adjusted against my credit card balance. 

Today I get a call saying there is a balance in my HDFC bank account. I was surprised because I don’t use that account and don’t maintain any balance. Then they told me that the amount of the Airbnb booking, which was cancelled, was credit back to my bank account and then some outstanding dues were clawed back from that amount. 

Now so many questions: 
1. How does a credit card transaction reversal get credited to a bank account? 
2. How does the credit card statement show the reversal, and has it actually been adjusted against my credit card balance? 
3. Has HDFC credited money into the account by error while also adjusting it against my credit card balance? Which means they’ve given me some extra money. 

Visited the local branch, and they were nice enough to understand this and raise a ticket. But I’m yet to get answers.

text:
#HDFC 

The system has truly come of age. No longer does our regulator takes these things lightly.

In the HDFC / MSRDC issue, three senior officers of @HDFC_Bank have been visited with a disproportionately large penalty: ₹1 lakh each.

@SJagdishan (MD & CEO), Srinivasan Vaidyanathan (CFO) and Arvind Vohra (Group Head – Retail Assets) now face this crushing burden. One wonders how they will manage their daily bread, rice and dal, leave alone school fees of their children and family obligations.

How rather naive of Sashi, if only he had known the penalty would be this harsh for such a small indiscretion, he could perhaps have used this particular tool of overreach - which some people are, rather crudely and stupidly, calling bribery - more freely and on a wider scale across the country. Far larger deposits might have been generated. The long-standing lovers of HDFC Bank would then not have had to endure the languishing share price for quite so long.

Targets, after all, exist to be met. Preferential treatment to a large government client, even if it quietly disadvantaged ordinary retail depositors who trusted the bank with their life savings, remains in the grand scheme a relatively minor administrative matter.
Surely a more compassionate fine was possible.

#HDFCBank #MSRDC #BankingGovernance #RBI #CorporateAccountability @HDFC_Bank 

What really happened 
#MSRDC, a Maharashtra government body, was sitting on a very large pile of money - reports spoke of over ₹20,000 crore that banks were competing to attract as deposits. HDFC Bank wanted a share of that money. The difficulty was that RBI rules do not allow banks to quietly offer higher interest rates to big clients. So, according to earlier reports, the bank found a creative way around it: roughly ₹45 crore was routed through the marketing budget and shown as “sponsorship” for road-safety campaigns. In effect, this was extra money paid to make the deposit deal more attractive without calling it higher interest or bribery.
That is the “business overreach” the board has now judged.

text:
Better to sell to recover your money. @HDFC_Bank is getting into more Fraud news and i am one of the victim. 

It lends 34.63 crores as Unsecured and even 20 crores without an agreement for company which not filed ITR in MCA portal beyond 2021 with a max turnover of around 90 crore per year. 

In June 2023, HDFC Bank made me guarantor for a ₹34,63,77,053 loan.

Without my consent. Without my KYC. Without my signature.

Three years later, my father is dead and I still don't have an answer. This is what happened.

The document that didn't exist

A Letter of Continuing Guarantee was created bearing a forged version of my signature. My PAN was mapped to a company-controlled email address on the NeSL statutory portal — a fabrication the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) confirmed to me in writing on 13.01.2026.

When I objected in writing, a second bank issued the takeover NOC anyway — later admitting in writing that it did so "due to repeated reminders from HDFC Bank."

One falsehood. Four institutions.

To the Central Crime Branch, Chennai: no document bears her signature. → Closure report, 07.02.2024.

To the Madras High Court: same. → Favourable order, 31.01.2025.

To the Reserve Bank of India: a different loan-application date than it filed in court. A different Board Resolution than it filed in court. And in July 2025 — "not a guarantor" — while the guarantee naming me sat in its own custody. → My complaint closed.

Then, in July 2026, two days before my RBI appeal hearing, HDFC produced that very Letter of Continuing Guarantee.

By its own hand, it proved every one of those statements false.

Section 46 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 makes furnishing wilfully false information to the RBI a punishable offence.

100+ complaints. Not one document ever verified.

Since 2023 my family has filed over 100 complaints — police, RBI, CPGRAMS, DPG, National Consumer Helpline, courts.

RBI's own Complaint Management System records 15 against HDFC and connected entities. First one: 12.06.2024.

Every single one closed.

Every closure based on the bank's own response — which no authority ever checked against a single document.

In three years, across a hundred complaints, not one authority asked HDFC to produce the guarantee it claimed to hold. The one document that would have ended this at the start.

And it kept lending

HDFC's own NeSL filings show money continued to move after my written fraud alert of 09.08.2023 — including a fresh cash credit of ₹5,49,91,000 on 17.09.2025.

The same filings record: "No authentication done by any parties till now."

What it cost

On 02.08.2026 my father — Shri Suresh Kumar K.A., 68, an accountant who stood beside me for three years, who lost his own ancestral home to a bank auction in the middle of this — died of a sudden cardiac arrest. The matter still unresolved.

We were a family of nine. We are eight.

Where it stands

I filed my rejoinder before the RBI Appellate Authority on 31.07.2026. I wrote again a month after the hearing.

No order. No acknowledgement. Silence.

I'm not asking anyone to take my word. Every line above is on the record — in the banks' own written admissions, in RBI's own complaint database, in IBBI's own confirmation letter.

I'm asking one question:

If a bank can manufacture a ₹34 crore liability against a citizen who never signed anything, hide the evidence from a criminal court, and face no consequence across 100 complaints and 3 years — what protects any of us?

text:
My Response to HDFC Bank

Thank you for acknowledging my feedback. However, I believe that simply forwarding a customer's concerns to the relevant team is not enough when the issue involves investor confidence, transparency and the long-term credibility of a major institution like HDFC Bank.

If customers and investors raise genuine concerns, they deserve to know what specific steps are being taken, what areas are being improved, and what measurable changes they can expect.

A strong institution should not hide behind general statements. Transparency is the foundation of trust. If there are weaknesses in management, customer service, digital banking, communication or investor relations, they should be openly identified and addressed.

I am not asking HDFC Bank to protect its share price artificially. I am asking the institution to strengthen the fundamentals that naturally create long-term value and investor confidence.

My suggestion is simple:

1. Clearly identify the key areas that require improvement.
2. Share a transparent roadmap for addressing those issues.
3. Communicate progress regularly with customers and investors.
4. Strengthen management accountability and service quality.
5. Explain clearly how these improvements will benefit customers, shareholders and the wider Indian economy.

HDFC Bank is one of India's most important financial institutions. Therefore, its responsibility is much greater than simply responding to individual customer complaints.

If HDFC wants to build stronger trust, let the market and the public see the improvement—not just hear that the feedback has been forwarded.

I hope the management will take this feedback seriously and respond with concrete actions rather than a standard customer-care response.

I am fighting for 3 years for an FIR against Partners and @HDFC_Bank 

In June 2023, HDFC Bank made me guarantor for a ₹34,63,77,053 loan.

Without my consent. Without my KYC. Without my signature.

Three years later, my father is dead and I still don't have an answer. This is what happened.

The document that didn't exist

A Letter of Continuing Guarantee was created bearing a forged version of my signature. My PAN was mapped to a company-controlled email address on the NeSL statutory portal — a fabrication the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) confirmed to me in writing on 13.01.2026.

When I objected in writing, a second bank issued the takeover NOC anyway — later admitting in writing that it did so "due to repeated reminders from HDFC Bank."

One falsehood. Four institutions.

To the Central Crime Branch, Chennai: no document bears her signature. → Closure report, 07.02.2024.

To the Madras High Court: same. → Favourable order, 31.01.2025.

To the Reserve Bank of India: a different loan-application date than it filed in court. A different Board Resolution than it filed in court. And in July 2025 — "not a guarantor" — while the guarantee naming me sat in its own custody. → My complaint closed.

Then, in July 2026, two days before my RBI appeal hearing, HDFC produced that very Letter of Continuing Guarantee.

By its own hand, it proved every one of those statements false.

Section 46 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 makes furnishing wilfully false information to the RBI a punishable offence.

100+ complaints. Not one document ever verified.

Since 2023 my family has filed over 100 complaints — police, RBI, CPGRAMS, DPG, National Consumer Helpline, courts.

RBI's own Complaint Management System records 15 against HDFC and connected entities. First one: 12.06.2024.

Every single one closed.

Every closure based on the bank's own response — which no authority ever checked against a single document.

In three years, across a hundred complaints, not one authority asked HDFC to produce the guarantee it claimed to hold. The one document that would have ended this at the start.

And it kept lending

HDFC's own NeSL filings show money continued to move after my written fraud alert of 09.08.2023 — including a fresh cash credit of ₹5,49,91,000 on 17.09.2025.

The same filings record: "No authentication done by any parties till now."

What it cost

On 02.08.2026 my father — Shri Suresh Kumar K.A., 68, an accountant who stood beside me for three years, who lost his own ancestral home to a bank auction in the middle of this — died of a sudden cardiac arrest. The matter still unresolved.

We were a family of nine. We are eight.

Where it stands

I filed my rejoinder before the RBI Appellate Authority on 31.07.2026. I wrote again a month after the hearing.

No order. No acknowledgement. Silence.

I'm not asking anyone to take my word. Every line above is on the record — in the banks' own written admissions, in RBI's own complaint database, in IBBI's own confirmation letter.

I'm asking one question:

If a bank can manufacture a ₹34 crore liability against a citizen who never signed anything, hide the evidence from a criminal court, and face no consequence across 100 complaints and 3 years — what protects any of us?

text:
Nothing wrong from the bank’s side.The system calculates dues down to the last paisa. Whatever outstanding balance you have on the credit card statement (including principal, interest, and fees), you are required to pay the exact amount.
You paid 10,649 and deliberately left out 46 paise. That means your outstanding balance was not fully cleared.  In credit card systems, even a shortfall of a few paise is treated as a partial payment. 
Once the due date passes without the full amount being settled, the system automatically flags it as a late payment and applies the late payment fee as per the card’s terms and conditions.  
This is standard banking practice systems do not round off or ignore small balances. The 46 paise shortfall triggered the late fee correctly. 
Why are you crying now?

text: Rounding off applies to Bank charges such as interest and late payment charges. Here, the Bank has charged this guy a late payment charge of INR 1200 which is very much a round figure. What you are referring to round off the billed amount to ₹10,649.00 is the principle amount. The RBI circular doesn't say that Banks must round down the principle amount and suffer a loss of 46 paise. HDFC Bank have over 12 crore customers and rounding down on the principle amount would mean a loss of over 5 crore rupees. Rules are for every one.

Positives for .@HDFC_Bank 

1. Fresh leadership cycle – A new CEO can bring fresh thinking after the long HDFC Bank/merger transition period.

2. Opportunity to reset growth strategy – The bank has grown the balance sheet strongly, but margins have been under pressure. A new leader could focus more sharply on ROA, NIM and profitable growth. 

3. Post-merger phase is largely behind it – The next CEO inherits a much more integrated HDFC Bank and can concentrate on extracting the full benefits of the HDFC Ltd merger rather than managing the transition.

4. Succession can reduce key-person dependence – A smooth transition demonstrates that HDFC Bank is institutionally strong and not dependent on one individual.

5. Potentially more aggressive retail strategy – There could be a renewed push on CASA, credit cards, mortgages, SME and cross-selling, areas where investors may want stronger execution.

6. Fresh capital-allocation discipline – A new CEO may reassess the balance between growth, margins, provisions and capital efficiency, potentially improving ROA/ROE over the medium term.

7. Positive governance signal – Given Sashi’s nearly three-decade association with HDFC Bank, a planned succession rather than an abrupt departure gives the board an opportunity to demonstrate strong succession planning.

text:
Its not #Friction its #Facts 

I am one of the Victim of @HDFC_Bank #Fraud #forgery #Fabrication #misrepresentation 

I lost my Father because of this Fraud #HDFC who stood with me 3 years to Fight Against 35 crore Borrower and Guarantor without consent. Lost his belief because of the Failure of @RBI @DFS_India @cpgrams Governance 

In June 2023, HDFC Bank made me guarantor for a ₹34,63,77,053 loan.

Without my consent. Without my KYC. Without my signature.

Three years later, my father is dead and I still don't have an answer. This is what happened.

The document that didn't exist

A Letter of Continuing Guarantee was created bearing a forged version of my signature. My PAN was mapped to a company-controlled email address on the NeSL statutory portal — a fabrication the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) confirmed to me in writing on 13.01.2026.

When I objected in writing, a second bank issued the takeover NOC anyway — later admitting in writing that it did so "due to repeated reminders from HDFC Bank."

One falsehood. Four institutions.

To the Central Crime Branch, Chennai: no document bears her signature. → Closure report, 07.02.2024.

To the Madras High Court: same. → Favourable order, 31.01.2025.

To the Reserve Bank of India: a different loan-application date than it filed in court. A different Board Resolution than it filed in court. And in July 2025 — "not a guarantor" — while the guarantee naming me sat in its own custody. → My complaint closed.

Then, in July 2026, two days before my RBI appeal hearing, HDFC produced that very Letter of Continuing Guarantee.

By its own hand, it proved every one of those statements false.

Section 46 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 makes furnishing wilfully false information to the RBI a punishable offence.

100+ complaints. Not one document ever verified.

Since 2023 my family has filed over 100 complaints — police, RBI, CPGRAMS, DPG, National Consumer Helpline, courts.

RBI's own Complaint Management System records 15 against HDFC and connected entities. First one: 12.06.2024.

Every single one closed.

Every closure based on the bank's own response — which no authority ever checked against a single document.

In three years, across a hundred complaints, not one authority asked HDFC to produce the guarantee it claimed to hold. The one document that would have ended this at the start.

And it kept lending

HDFC's own NeSL filings show money continued to move after my written fraud alert of 09.08.2023 — including a fresh cash credit of ₹5,49,91,000 on 17.09.2025.

The same filings record: "No authentication done by any parties till now."

What it cost

On 02.08.2026 my father — Shri Suresh Kumar K.A., 68, an accountant who stood beside me for three years, who lost his own ancestral home to a bank auction in the middle of this — died of a sudden cardiac arrest. The matter still unresolved.

We were a family of nine. We are eight.

Where it stands

I filed my rejoinder before the RBI Appellate Authority on 31.07.2026. I wrote again a month after the hearing.

No order. No acknowledgement. Silence.

I'm not asking anyone to take my word. Every line above is on the record — in the banks' own written admissions, in RBI's own complaint database, in IBBI's own confirmation letter.

I'm asking one question:

If a bank can manufacture a ₹34 crore liability against a citizen who never signed anything, hide the evidence from a criminal court, and face no consequence across 100 complaints and 3 years — what protects any of us?

text:
I would like to share my own experience. I currently have a personal loan from @HDFC_Bank with an EMI of ₹27,671, which gets debited from my @TheOfficialSBI Savings Bank Account on the 6th-7th of every month.

This month, accidentally, I paid my room rent from my SBI account on 5th August, due to which the EMI debit failed. Although I paid the EMI on the very next day, 6th August, using my other bank account, @TheOfficialSBI charged me ₹295 and @HDFC_Bank charged me ₹450.

I called both banks requesting a refund, considering my good repayment track record and the fact that my EMI had never bounced before. But both banks categorically refused to refund the charges.

Banks follow every rule strictly when dealing with common people, but treat those seeking a 99.87% haircut on a ₹30,000 crore loan very differently.

Waah Indian Banking System. Waah @RBI.

text:
@HDFC_Bank creates the documents as required they don't even need consent or Networth. They need a scapegoat, here the scapegoat is investors

In June 2023, HDFC Bank made me guarantor for a ₹34,63,77,053 loan.

Without my consent. Without my KYC. Without my signature.

Three years later, my father is dead and I still don't have an answer. This is what happened.

The document that didn't exist

A Letter of Continuing Guarantee was created bearing a forged version of my signature. My PAN was mapped to a company-controlled email address on the NeSL statutory portal — a fabrication the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) confirmed to me in writing on 13.01.2026.

When I objected in writing, a second bank issued the takeover NOC anyway — later admitting in writing that it did so "due to repeated reminders from HDFC Bank."

One falsehood. Four institutions.

To the Central Crime Branch, Chennai: no document bears her signature. → Closure report, 07.02.2024.

To the Madras High Court: same. → Favourable order, 31.01.2025.

To the Reserve Bank of India: a different loan-application date than it filed in court. A different Board Resolution than it filed in court. And in July 2025 — "not a guarantor" — while the guarantee naming me sat in its own custody. → My complaint closed.

Then, in July 2026, two days before my RBI appeal hearing, HDFC produced that very Letter of Continuing Guarantee.

By its own hand, it proved every one of those statements false.

Section 46 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 makes furnishing wilfully false information to the RBI a punishable offence.

100+ complaints. Not one document ever verified.

Since 2023 my family has filed over 100 complaints — police, RBI, CPGRAMS, DPG, National Consumer Helpline, courts.

RBI's own Complaint Management System records 15 against HDFC and connected entities. First one: 12.06.2024.

Every single one closed.

Every closure based on the bank's own response — which no authority ever checked against a single document.

In three years, across a hundred complaints, not one authority asked HDFC to produce the guarantee it claimed to hold. The one document that would have ended this at the start.

And it kept lending

HDFC's own NeSL filings show money continued to move after my written fraud alert of 09.08.2023 — including a fresh cash credit of ₹5,49,91,000 on 17.09.2025.

The same filings record: "No authentication done by any parties till now."

What it cost

On 02.08.2026 my father — Shri Suresh Kumar K.A., 68, an accountant who stood beside me for three years, who lost his own ancestral home to a bank auction in the middle of this — died of a sudden cardiac arrest. The matter still unresolved.

We were a family of nine. We are eight.

Where it stands

I filed my rejoinder before the RBI Appellate Authority on 31.07.2026. I wrote again a month after the hearing.

No order. No acknowledgement. Silence.

I'm not asking anyone to take my word. Every line above is on the record — in the banks' own written admissions, in RBI's own complaint database, in IBBI's own confirmation letter.

I'm asking one question:

If a bank can manufacture a ₹34 crore liability against a citizen who never signed anything, hide the evidence from a criminal court, and face no consequence across 100 complaints and 3 years — what protects any of us?

text:
“Third-party product” does not mean “no responsibility” for the Bank.

The key questions are:

🔹 Who approved the product for distribution?
🔹 Who pitched it to the customer? HDFC Bank employees.
🔹 Who did the customer trust? The Bank and its employees.
🔹 Did the Bank/its employees receive distribution fees, commissions or incentives?
🔹 Was the product's risk and liquidity clearly explained?

Customers don't generally approach a complex investment product independently—they often rely on the credibility of the Bank and its Relationship Manager.

If the Bank benefited financially from distributing the product, then simply saying “the fund house is responsible” does not answer the questions of due diligence, suitability, sales practices and customer protection.

Third party may explain who managed the fund.
It does not automatically answer who is accountable for how the product was sold.

text:
Kotak Sec note:

*Kotak Updates*

.@HDFC_Bank (BUY, FV Rs1050)
- Company that current MD and CEO, Mr Sashidhar Jagdishan, has decided not to seek reappointment upon completion of his current term. This marks a leadership transition at the bank, with the board indicating that it has accelerated the succession process and intends to appoint a successor well ahead of the transition.
- We maintain BUY with an unchanged FV of Rs1,050 while retaining our estimates. *Although the current valuations appear undemanding, the evolving developments at the bank continue to constrain confidence in a durable long-term investment case.* Nonetheless, the underlying fundamentals remain intact. The liability franchise, while weaker than best-in-class peers, continues to grow at a healthy pace relative to most Indian banks. *In our view, only a modest strategic course correction is needed to rebuild investor confidence. Until the confidence improves, we expect the current valuation discount to persist.*

*MSCI August Rebal*
- There are 4 addition and 3 deletion this time to the MSCI India index. LAURUS, LENSKART, ADANIENS and GROWW are getting added to the index while ASTRA, SBICARD and BIL getting deleted.
- Among weight changes – ETERNAL will see major weight increase due to adjustment of foreign room. In addition there will be weight increase in ADE, ADSEZ, JSW while there will be weight down in RELIANCE, JIOFIN, IH, ABCAP due to adjustment of free-float.

*OFS – Knowledge Realty*
- Launched ~Rs12000cr/US$1.25bn offer-for-sale in KNOWLEDGE REIT which closes for institutions TODAY

text:
Paid Rs.105411 on my @HDFC_Bank credit card this afternoon. Entered the OTP, payment went through, got the usual SMS. Done, or so I thought.

Within minutes the calls started. Then came the WhatsApp messages, not one but several, titled "Action Required: Transaction Confirmation", asking me to confirm the same payment I had just authorised with an OTP.

So here is my question for credit card companies. What exactly is the OTP for?

The whole point of two factor authentication is that the OTP is the confirmation. I have the card, I have the phone, I entered the code. If the bank still does not trust that, then the OTP is theatre and the real verification is a call centre agent asking me "Sir, did you make this transaction?"

Either the OTP confirms the transaction or it does not. Pick one.

What makes this worse is how little thought has gone into the risk model. A basic check of my own card history would show the same merchant name, similar amounts, paid multiple times before from the same card. Nothing about this transaction is new. No new device, no new location, no new merchant. Yet the system flagged it and I am the one being made to do the bank's homework.

This is not risk management. This is a rule that says "amount above X, pester the customer" and calling it fraud prevention.

And let us say something does go wrong. A fraudulent charge, goods not delivered, merchant vanishes. There is already a process for that. It is called chargeback and it exists precisely so the bank does not need to ring every customer after every large payment. Fraud and non delivery are covered. The customer has recourse. So the calls and the flood of messages add no protection, only disturbance.

There is another problem banks do not seem to notice. Every scam in India today runs on the same script: an urgent message, "action required", confirm your transaction, click here, call this number. Now the bank's own genuine messages look exactly like the scam messages. When you train customers to respond to "Action Required" from a bank, you are making the scammer's job easier, not harder.

In short, the OTP should be the last word. If your risk engine cannot read a customer's own transaction history, fix the engine instead of outsourcing the checking to the customer. And if you are going to call and message anyway, stop pretending the OTP means anything.

@RBI, this deserves a look. Banks should not be allowed to treat "we disturbed the customer five times" as a fraud control.

text:
@HDFCBank_Cares @HDFC_Bank
@RBI
I have been an HDFC Bank customer since 2020.

My savings account was not used regularly after 2021, and due to non-maintenance of the required balance, charges have apparently accumulated over the years.

The account currently does not show a negative balance. However, when I add money to the account, a substantial amount of accumulated charges may be automatically deducted.

This creates a serious problem for customers who want to restart using their old bank accounts.

If charges of around ₹350/month have accumulated for several years, the amount can become significant — even though the customer may not have actively used the account during that period.

My concern is bigger than just my individual account.

How many old/inactive savings accounts across India may have accumulated such charges, making customers hesitant to start using them again?

RBI guidelines state that the balance in a savings account should not turn negative solely because of minimum-balance charges, and customers should be properly notified regarding such charges.

From a customer and business perspective, banks should consider a more customer-friendly approach for old/inactive accounts — especially when the customer wants to resume the relationship.

HDFC Bank, instead of simply recovering years of accumulated charges when the customer deposits money, should review such accounts and provide a reasonable resolution.

My request:

• Provide a complete year-wise breakup of all charges since 2021
• Confirm the basis and validity of each charge
• Confirm what notifications were sent regarding the shortfall
• Review and waive/reverse eligible accumulated charges
• Allow me to restart using my HDFC Bank account without an unreasonable financial burden

This is not only about recovering a few thousand rupees.

It is about customer retention, trust and long-term banking relationships.

@RBI
Please look into the broader customer-impact aspect of such practices.

#Stock, #Nifty50, #Banknifty
